The study of human chromosome structure is called cytogenetics. The banding techniques such as Q-banding and C-banding have made it possible to identify individual chromosomes and even to localize genes on the chromosomes.
A technique, which has greatly simplified the identification of individual chromosomes, is the use of a staining procedure first described by Joseph Gall in 1978 and referred to as the silver stain. This technique involves several steps. First, the chromosomes are briefly exposed to a hypotonic solution, which causes them to swell and lengthen. Then, the slides are incubated for several hours in a hot solution of silver nitrate, which is taken up by the DNA of the chromosomes. Finally, the slides are rinsed in a series of acetic acid solutions, which remove most of the silver not bound to the chromosomes, and then counterstained with a dye so that the chromosomes can be visualized under a microscope. Because this staining procedure produces sharply defined bands when the chromosomes are visualized under a microscope, the technique is commonly referred to as banding.
Two common types of banding procedures are the Q-banding technique, developed by Quinacrine, and the C-banding technique, developed by Cavalli and Garnier. In Q-banding, the chromosome goes through a process known as condensation, where segments of the long double helix of DNA become tightly wound and change from a lightly staining euchromatin to a more darkly staining heterochromatin. 
In C-banding, the chromosomes are digested with an enzyme called ceain endonucleases, which cause cuts in one or more of the DNA strands. These cuts result in the formation of giant chromocenters (aggregates of highly condensed chromatin material) at each centromere.
